1.pericope_label: Isaac blesses Jacob again and sends him to Padan-aram for a wife

schools.summary: Deny that the repetition implies the first blessing failed — it was efficacious, but faith needed the support, and Jacob had to be blessed knowingly this time lest the memory of the fraud unsettle him; treat Isaac’s part as prophetic prayer rather than conveyance; explain the personal journey as a way of sparing Esau’s envy; and read the promised assembly as one body gathered at last out of many nations.

Set the flight against the blessing — rich in promise and poor in fact, blessed with government and going out to service — and give two reasons for it, correction for the fraud and the persecution that follows the inheritance, adding that providence often seems to run counter to promise.

Argue from the stone pillow and the staff that Jacob travelled alone and unattended, dismissing the oil poured on the pillar as evidence of baggage; read “a multitude of people” as a church of peoples reaching beyond Israel to the Christian Church; and hold that those who have the blessing must keep the charge attached to it and not separate what God has joined.

Identify the blessing as the promise repeatedly given to Abraham and locate it; commend Isaac’s frankness in confirming the younger son without hedging; argue from Isaac’s knowledge of the Haran family that he sent his son in person rather than a deputy, and that Bethuel mattered more than the Rabbins allow; and distinguish the word for “assembly” from the one used in the covenant chapter.

debates: Whether Jacob travelled alone or attended — Clarke argues from the stone pillow and the staff that he had God alone with him, Gill that he was sent off in haste and alone, while Ellicott has him escorted to the caravan route and travelling on with a trading company.

Why the blessing is repeated at all: because the first was in itself sufficient and only Jacob’s faith needed support (Calvin), because he might otherwise doubt what he had got by subtlety (Clarke), or because it was one blessing stated generally and now particularised (Gill).

Why Isaac sent Jacob himself instead of a servant, as Abraham had done for Rebekah — to spare Esau’s envy (Calvin) or because Isaac knew the Haran family well enough to do without a deputy (Ellicott).

What “a multitude of people” promises — the tribes of Israel, the congregation in the wilderness, or a church gathered from many nations, with Ellicott resting the religious sense on the choice of word.
outliers: Clarke alone assembles the evidence for Jacob’s poverty on the road and states the conclusion as a bare sentence.
Calvin alone frames the repetition as a problem about prophetic authority before answering it.
Ellicott alone defends Bethuel’s standing against the rabbinic account of Laban’s prominence.
Henry alone turns the flight into a general rule about providence appearing to contradict promise.

6.pericope_label: Esau sees Jacob sent away, and marries a daughter of Ishmael

schools.summary: Defend the marriage as a sincere attempt to obey and please his parents against those who count it a crime, pressing the exact symmetry of the two matches; hold the chronology of Ishmael’s death open, since a shorter reckoning of Jacob’s age would let the text stand literally; and take the passage as showing the influence of a good example.

Read the marriage as the act of a man who wants the blessing without repenting, devising a strange method of reconciliation and seeking to propitiate his father rather than God, so that the episode paints every hypocrite to the life; and gather the incidental detail — what Esau may have understood the blessing to be, why Rebekah is unmentioned, and that it was Ishmael’s house and not Ishmael that he went to.

Offer the passage as either a lesson in the force of a good example or an instance of the folly of wisdom that comes too late, and then charge the marriage on three counts — the rejected family, the third wife taken while two remained, and the intention of pleasing a father rather than God in hope of a revised will.

Explain Esau’s motive from his grief at the transfer and his awareness that his own foreign marriages had caused it, and settle the identity of his new wife from the double naming and the description of her as the sister of Nebajoth.

debates: Whether Esau’s marriage was sincere obedience (Clarke), a hypocrite’s partial satisfaction (Calvin), well done but far too late and made worse in the doing (Henry), or simple conformity to a rule he now saw the force of (Ellicott).

Whether Ishmael was alive — the common computation puts his death fourteen years earlier, which forces “went unto Ishmael” to mean his house (Gill, and Clarke by that reckoning), while a shorter chronology of Jacob’s age would leave him living (Clarke).
Why the notice about Esau interrupts Jacob’s story at all: as a foil showing the power of example, or as an exhibition of repentance that reforms one fault and leaves the man unchanged.
outliers: Clarke alone defends Esau, and alone builds the defence on the symmetry between the two marriages.
Calvin alone turns the episode into a general anatomy of hypocritical satisfaction, and alone says it were better to be an obscure member of the Church than a great man outside it.
Henry alone counts the wives and objects that two were still living.
Ellicott alone works out which of Ishmael’s wives was the mother, from the repeated description of Mahalath as Nebajoth’s sister.

10.pericope_label: Jacob leaves Beersheba and lodges at the place, with a stone for his pillow

schools.summary: Compress the journey into a single day of above forty miles; dwell on the hardness and exposure of the lodging, and give three reasons other than poverty for it — the plainness of the age, Jacob’s habituation to hardship, and his confidence in the divine protection.

Measure the distance and deny that it could be covered in a day; argue from the eighteenth verse that there was only one stone; explain the open-air lodging by a traveller’s suspicion of a strange town or by city gates shut at nightfall; and keep, of the three reasons for his ease, only his confidence in God.

Send Jacob off alone but not unprovided, with letters from his parents and money enough for the road, the oil being the evidence; and read the whole exile as the Church preserved in one man, the dry trunk and the momentary green branch left behind while the severed twig is carried away to be kept alive by heaven.

Put the journey at four days at least and make the interval itself the preparation, the traveller drawing near to God as he goes; insist that the heir would not have been sent away without a few trusty servants; take “the place” as appointed though lighted on by chance; report the rabbinic identification with Moriah and the altar stone and set it aside as allegory; and note that the history of Isaac is in fact the history of Jacob from this point.

debates: How long the journey to Bethel took — one day of above forty miles (Henry), more than a day because the distance is forty-eight (Clarke, with Gill giving the same figure), or at least four days (Ellicott).

Whether Jacob travelled alone: alone but provisioned and carrying letters (Gill), alone and destitute on the evidence of the staff (Clarke), or with a few trusty servants, the staff proving nothing (Ellicott, answering that argument directly).
Why he slept in the open so near a town — suspicion of its inhabitants, or gates already shut for the night (Clarke), against the others who treat the lodging simply as the traveller’s lot.

What the definite article in “the place” signifies: a spot appointed beforehand for the revelation (Keil, Ellicott), and whether the rabbinic identification with Moriah and the altar stone can stand (Ellicott says it cannot).
outliers: Ellicott alone makes the length of the journey part of the argument, treating the four days as the meditation that prepared Jacob to be accepted.
Ellicott alone answers, and rejects, the argument from Jacob’s staff that the others build on.
Clarke alone explains the open-air lodging from the customs of walled towns rather than from Jacob’s poverty.
Calvin alone reads the departure as the survival of the Church in a single man, and alone draws the consolation that the wicked are left in possession meanwhile.

12.pericope_label: The ladder and the angels, and the promise spoken from above it

schools.summary: Read the ladder as three things at once — a figure of providence over all terrestrial things, the connection of the two worlds by angelic ministry, and a type of Christ in whom both natures meet — expounding the angels’ traffic in detail; and press the promise to its widest extent, the blessing reaching families outside Abraham’s line because Christ tasted death for every man, none being excluded who do not exclude themselves.

Deny outright that the ladder is a figure of providence, and subordinate the vision to the oracle on the ground that mute visions are cold and the word quickens them, turning this against sacraments that carry no voice; read Jacob’s destitution as the discipline that taught him to depend on the word alone; make him the fountain of blessing rather than its example; and take his never possessing the land as proof that something better was pledged under it.

Expound the vision itself — heaven and earth joined and a way opened between them, the messengers carrying prayers up and help down, and Jehovah taking a permanent and not an accidental station at the head — noting the threefold “behold” that builds to its climax there.

debates: Whether the ladder figures divine providence — asserted as its primary design by Clarke and elaborated by Wesley, admitted in a limited form by Gill, and expressly rejected by Calvin as an interpretation that cannot be admitted.

Whether the weight of the passage lies in the vision or in the words spoken from above it, Calvin making the figure an appendage to the promise where Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott expound the figure at length.
How far the blessing of the nations extends and on what ground — Clarke and Wesley to every family without exception, Calvin by making Jacob the fountain rather than the pattern of blessing.
What the gift of a land Jacob never held implies: Calvin infers a better thing pledged under the earnest, where the others take the promise at its face.
outliers: Calvin alone rejects the providential reading of the ladder, and alone uses the vision to argue against silent sacraments.
Ellicott alone rests an argument on the verb used of Jehovah standing at the head, and alone notices the threefold “behold”.
Clarke alone collects the Targum and the Greek renderings of the promise of presence.
Calvin alone finds significance in Jacob’s never being allowed even to die in the land promised him.

16.pericope_label: Jacob awakes: surely the LORD is in this place, and how dreadful is this place

schools.summary: Take the place as God’s peculiar residence, already consecrated for all Jacob knew, and report the Targum’s reading that the gate of heaven lay directly above it, which Jacob himself seems to have believed; suppose Jacob’s mind already humbled and so prepared for communion; and set his fear against any temptation to be puffed up by the revelation.

Explain the surprise not by ignorance of omnipresence but by distance from the known shrines, Jacob feeling cut off from the religion of his youth; make the point of the dream that Jehovah watches the whole earth; and distinguish the awe and dread of a manifestation from fear.

Deny that any place holds the honour, since Christ has filled the world with his presence, and turn the verse against those who claim it for their temples; hold that God presented himself to one who was not seeking him and gave more than he dared hope; and distinguish the fear that produces pious submission from the terror of the reprobate.

Note that the revelation came while Jacob was asleep and passive, grace not waiting on the sons of men, and that God is met where he was not looked for, no place excluding a visit; and read the fear as the mark of a man kept low in his own eyes by what he had seen.

debates: Whether the place was itself holy — Clarke has God making it his peculiar residence and reports a tradition locating the gate of heaven above it, while Calvin, Ellicott and Wesley all deny that any place carries the honour.
Whether Jacob was prepared for the vision: Clarke supposes his mind already humbled and ready for communion, Calvin insists God came to one who sought him not and gave beyond his hope.

What kind of fear the verse records — filial and not servile (Gill), submission and not terror (Calvin), awe and dread but not fear (Ellicott) — a distinction all four draw and none draws in quite the same words.
How much of the meeting was Jacob’s doing: Henry stresses that it came while he slept and was purely passive, against readings that make the preceding journey a preparation.
outliers: Clarke alone treats the locality as genuinely privileged, and alone reports Onkelos placing the opening of heaven physically above the spot.
Calvin alone turns the phrase “the gate of heaven” against the consecration of church buildings.
Ellicott alone explains Jacob’s surprise by his distance from the shrines his family used, naming one in the neighbourhood.
Gill alone insists on the adjective, that the fear was filial and not servile, and that it carried no distrust of the assurance just given.

18.pericope_label: Jacob sets up the stone, pours oil on it, and calls the place Bethel

schools.summary: Take the pillar as a marker of the spot and a means of finding it again to pay vows there, the oil being the ordinary symbol of dedication and expressly not an act of worship offered to the stone; and argue from the wording that the new name was given to the neighbouring town rather than to the open ground, or else that town and holy place were distinct and the name migrated later.

Take the rising and the naming at their plain sense; defend the pillar against the charge of idolatry by distinguishing memorial from image, and read the oil as testifying that nothing is holy which the Spirit has not sanctified, while declining the reading that makes the stone a symbol of Christ; deny that the city yet existed; and close with the later corruption of Bethel as proof that the example of a patriarch is no warrant without a command.

Treat the anointed stone as an altar in effect, and set it in the long history of anointed stones and images among the nations, from which the consecrated stones of antiquity and much of image-worship descend; report the tradition that identifies this stone with the one under the coronation chair while refusing to argue for it; and explain the pillar as a substitute for the altar Jacob had no time to build.

debates: What the anointing did — consecrated the stone as an altar fit for libation and sacrifice (Clarke), or marked a memorial that was expressly not an object of worship (Keil, Calvin, and in effect Ellicott and Wesley).
Whether Bethel and Luz were the same place: Keil takes the name to be given to the town, Ellicott holds the two were distinct and near, and Calvin denies that any town existed there yet.
Whether the stone is to be read as a figure of Christ, which Calvin reports of other commentators and rejects.
What the practice of anointing stones proves — Clarke traces the idolatry of the nations back to this act, where Calvin uses the same prohibition to show that Jacob’s act was of a different kind.
outliers: Clarke alone connects the pillar to the anointed stones of the nations and makes Jacob’s act the historical root of their superstition.
Clarke alone reports the tradition of the stone’s travels to Westminster, and alone refuses either to defend or refute it.
Calvin alone denies that the city existed at the time, and alone draws from Bethel’s later history the rule that a patriarch’s example is no warrant.
Ellicott alone argues that the place where Jacob slept was not the site of the town that later bore the name.

20.pericope_label: Jacob vows a vow: if God will be with me, then the LORD shall be my God

schools.summary: Defend vows against both the rash and the fastidious by three tests, and show Jacob meeting all of them, before turning the passage against the vows of Rome; keep the condition on Jacob himself and answer the charge that he promises beyond his strength by appeal to pardon through the Spirit; and divide the vow into worship, rite and charitable oblation, noting that this is the first vow in Scripture and that the heathen later copied the tithe.

Refer the vow to Jacob’s posterity rather than to himself, on the ground that it answers the promises about his offspring and removes the appearance of self-interest, and read the whole flight and return as a type of the exodus and settlement; and defend tithes at length as a divinely instituted and reasonable provision, with an express disclaimer of personal interest.

Rest the sense of the condition on the alternation of the divine names, the protasis using “God” where the rest uses “the LORD”, so that the vow turns on Jehovah proving himself to be God by fulfilling what he promised.

Take the vow as a pattern of faith, moderation and piety — Jacob asking neither soft clothing nor dainty meat — and draw from it that abundance obliges thankfulness and scarcity contentment, with the tenth as a fit but not a rigid proportion.

debates: Whether the vow binds Jacob or his descendants — Clarke argues for posterity, partly because Scripture never records Jacob performing it, while Calvin and Keil read it of Jacob himself.
Whether a conditional vow of lifelong fidelity promises more than a man can perform, and how Calvin answers that it does not because pardon is embraced along with the promise.
Whether vows are lawful at all, Calvin steering between those who make them indiscriminately and those who disallow them entirely.

What the tithe is for and where it comes from — a divine institution matched to the maintenance of a landless tribe (Clarke), a threefold duty ending in charity (Calvin), or a proportion later imitated by the heathen (Gill).
outliers: Clarke alone displaces the vow onto Jacob’s posterity, and alone reads the exile and return as a type of the exodus.
Clarke alone interrupts his defence of tithes to declare that he has never received any.
Keil alone rests the interpretation on the change of divine name between the condition and its consequence.
Gill alone notes that this is the first vow in the Bible, and alone traces the tenth into pagan practice.
